title: A Bronze Age disc was stamped sign by sign, like printing, and no one can read it

cover.alt: The Phaistos Disc on a museum stand: a round, reddish-brown clay disc covered in small stamped pictures of heads, figures and rosettes arranged in a spiral.

body: In 1908 the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found a disc of fired clay, about 16 cm across, in the Minoan palace of Phaistos on Crete. Its two sides carry 242 signs of 45 different kinds, laid out in a spiral. Each one was made by pressing a separate stamp into the soft clay before firing, so the disc can be seen as an early example of movable-type printing. But the script and language are unknown. Despite many attempts at decipherment, no one can read it, and it is not even certain that it is writing at all.

slides.alt: The stone foundations, paved courts and wide staircase of the ruined Minoan palace of Phaistos, looking out over a green plain to mountains.
slides.caption: The ruins of the Minoan palace at Phaistos, where the disc turned up in 1908. It probably dates from the middle or late Minoan Bronze Age.

slides.prompt: The text spirals around both faces. Which way do scholars think it should be read?
slides.answer: Clockwise, from the rim to the centre
slides.detail: The archaeologist Arthur Evans first argued for reading from the centre outwards, but later changed his mind.

slides.label: times the commonest sign, a plumed head, appears
slides.text: Fourteen of them are on side A. Side A has 123 signs in all and side B 119.

slides.heading: Real or fake?
slides.text: Because of its unique features, some early scholars suspected a forgery or a hoax. Archaeologists now generally accept the disc as authentic. It is on display at the Heraklion Archaeological Museum in Crete.

slides.heading: What do we actually know?
slides.explanation: We know where it was found and how it was made. Its script and language are unknown, and it may not be writing at all.
